title: Speaker-Attested Grounding for False Memory Resistance in Agent Memory Systems

contributions.purpose: Diagnose why agent memory systems store false memories.
contributions.mechanism: Identifies assistant-originated self-verification: because the full dialogue is used as the evidence corpus, assistant-generated statements can serve as evidence for their own verification during memory filtering.
contributions.evaluation: Framed as the root-cause failure mode behind interference memories observed on the HaluMem benchmark.
contributions.domain: Agent memory systems / false memory storage
contributions.source_quote: We identify assistant-originated self-verification as a root cause of false memory storage in agent memory systems, where assistant statements serve as evidence for their own verification.

contributions.purpose: Provide a minimal intervention that increases resistance to false memories.
contributions.mechanism: Speaker-Attested Grounding (SAG) restricts the evidence corpus to user turns only during memory filtering while retaining full-dialogue extraction; a single-variable change to evidence construction.
contributions.evaluation: On HaluMem, improves False Memory Resistance by +11.94 percentage points (58.76% to 70.70%), with a moderate recall tradeoff of -7.20pp.
contributions.source_quote: We propose Speaker-Attested Grounding (SAG), a minimal single-variable intervention that improves False Memory Resistance by +11.94 percentage points on the HaluMem benchmark.

contributions.purpose: Confirm the gains come from the intended mechanism.
contributions.mechanism: Per-source analysis decomposing FMR gains by memory type (assistant-only vs user-repeated interference).
contributions.evaluation: 100% of FMR gains come from assistant-only interference memories, with no change on user-repeated interference.
contributions.source_quote: We demonstrate that SAG's improvements are precisely targeted: 100% of FMR gains come from assistant-only interference memories, with no change on user-repeated interference.

contributions.purpose: Separate the contribution of the speaker restriction itself from the confound of reduced evidence length.
contributions.mechanism: Ablation isolating the speaker restriction mechanism against length-matched baselines.
contributions.evaluation: 47.5% of gains come from the speaker restriction and 52.5% from reduced evidence length; SAG achieves a more favorable recall-FMR tradeoff than length-matched baselines.
contributions.source_quote: We provide ablation analysis isolating the speaker restriction mechanism (47.5% of gains) from evidence length effects (52.5%), showing that SAG achieves a more favorable recall-FMR tradeoff than length-matched baselines.

self_declared_provenance.quote: However, existing approaches use the full dialogue as evidence for filtering, which allows assistant-originated content to influence verification decisions-a design choice that our work specifically addresses.

Our work applies this grounding principle specifically to memory filtering: rather than verifying against the full dialogue, SAG restricts evidence to user turns only, preventing assistant-originated content from self-verifying false memories.

notes: Not a negative-result paper, but reports an explicit tradeoff: SAG's +11.94pp False Memory Resistance gain comes with a -7.20pp recall cost, and the ablation attributes only 47.5% of gains to the core speaker-restriction mechanism (52.5% to the confound of reduced evidence length).
